summary.title: Introduction to Secure Coding Guide (Apple Developer Archive)
summary.one_liner: Learn why security must be designed into software from the start and which vulnerability classes (buffer overflows, input validation, race conditions, privilege elevation, UI and helper design) Apple's guide covers for macOS and iOS developers.
takeaways: Security must be planned into software from the beginning; bolting it on later often requires redesign.
Common vulnerability classes covered include buffer overflows, unvalidated input, race conditions, and unsafe privilege elevation.
Apple's guide adds guidance on secure UI design and on designing helpers and daemons for privilege separation.
A pre-ship security development checklist is provided in an appendix.
Related references include Viega and McGraw's Building Secure Software, Wheeler's Secure Programming HOWTO, and OWASP.
summary.summary: This is the introduction to Apple's archived Secure Coding Guide, aimed at developers writing software for macOS and iOS. It argues that secure coding matters for all software and that threats must be identified and addressed throughout planning and development. It then outlines the document's structure, with chapters on specific vulnerability types (buffer overflows, input validation, race conditions and file operations, privilege elevation, secure UI, and helper/daemon design) plus checklists. It also points to external books and API references for networking, authorization, certificates, and keychain storage. The page is a conceptual overview with no code samples in the text shown.
